parts.move: state the centre of mass definition and what single force represents its effect
parts.prompt: Define the centre of mass of an object, and state what the weight of an object can be treated as for most mechanics purposes.
scheme: The centre of mass is the point through which the line of action of the weight acts for all orientations
Equivalently the average position of the mass, weighted by distance
Weight acts as if concentrated at the centre of mass
parts.answer: The centre of mass is the point where an object's weight is effectively concentrated — the average position of its mass. For any posture, gravity pulls through this one point, which is why balancing is about parking it over the base.

parts.move: state the moment of a force and why the perpendicular distance is the lever arm
parts.prompt: State the formula for the moment of a force about a pivot and define the distance used in it.
scheme: Moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action
It is the turning effect: F d sinθ between the force and the line from pivot to point
parts.answer: Moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action. Only the component across the radius turns a lever, so the perpendicular distance — never the straight-line distance to where the force is applied — is the lever arm.

parts.move: explain the tipping condition through the centre of mass and base of support
parts.prompt: A wrestler crouches with feet wide apart. Explain, using the centre of mass and the base of support, why this posture is hard to topple.
scheme: Tipping begins when the weight's line of action falls outside the base
A low centre of mass must be lifted as it moves sideways, raising gravitational PE
A wide base means a larger horizontal shift is needed to pass the line of action outside
parts.answer: To tip an object, its centre of mass must pass beyond the edge of the support base. Crouching drops the centre of mass so toppling must lift it — costing gravitational energy — and spreading the feet widens the base so more sideways push is needed to move the weight-line outside. Both make the wrestler a heavier proposition to fell.

parts.move: explain why limb muscles exert forces far above the load they hold
parts.prompt: A dumbbell held in the hand is far easier to support than the biceps force is large. Explain this in terms of lever arms about the elbow.
scheme: The biceps attaches centimetres from the elbow; the dumbbell acts tens of centimetres away
Moments must balance: F_biceps × d_biceps = W_load × d_load
The tiny muscle lever arm must be offset by a correspondingly huge muscle force
parts.answer: The elbow is the pivot: the dumbbell's weight acts on a long arm, the biceps on a short one. Moment balance, F×d_load, demands a muscle force in the same proportion as the arms are long — typically six to eight times the dumbbell's weight. Muscles trade force for speed and range, and joints pay in load.

parts.move: apply moment balance in a sports posture to find a support force
parts.prompt: A 60 kg gymnast holds a straight body horizontal, supported by hands and toes, with her centre of mass 0.90 m from her feet and 1.50 m from her hands. Calculate the force in her hands. (g = 9.81 m s⁻²)
scheme: Take moments about the toes: W × 0.90 = F_hands × 1.50
The remaining 236 N passes through the toes
parts.answer: Balancing moments about the toes: 589×0.90 = F×1.50, so the hands carry 353 N and the toes the rest — about 236 N. Choosing the toes as pivot erases the unknown toe force: the free-body trick of picking the pivot wisely.

parts.move: compute the shifted centre of mass of a combined body-plus-load system
parts.prompt: A 50 kg hiker carries a 15 kg pack whose centre of mass sits 0.30 m behind the hiker's own centre of mass. Calculate how far the combined centre of mass shifts backward, and why hikers lean forward.
scheme: Shift = (m_load × separation)/(m_total) = 15×0.30/65
= 0.069 m ≈ 7 cm backward
The weight line must stay over the feet for balance
Leaning forward moves the body's COM ahead to cancel the shift
parts.answer: The combined centre of mass moves 15×0.30/65 ≈ 7 cm toward the pack. To keep the weight line over his feet, the hiker leans forward — the visible price of a heavy pack is a compensating lean, and the shift formula is why the lean grows with pack weight.

parts.move: reject the claim that the centre of mass must lie within the material of an object
parts.prompt: A student says the centre of mass must be inside a high jumper's body, so clearing a bar higher than the COM is impossible. Correct the error and explain how elite jumpers clear bars above their centre of mass.
scheme: The centre of mass can lie outside the material — hollow or bent shapes have their COM in the gap
The arched 'Fosbury' posture places the COM partly under the bar while the body passes over
With the COM passing below the bar, less energy is needed than body-height lifting suggests
parts.answer: The centre of mass is an average position, not a piece of matter: a boomerang's COM sits in the air between its arms. The Fosbury arch curves the body so the COM threads beneath the bar while every segment clears above it — elite athletes lift their bodies over bars that beat their own centre of mass.

parts.move: separate a couple's pure turning effect from single-force moment balance
parts.prompt: A student says when you turn a tap with both hands the two equal opposite forces cancel, so no moment is produced. Identify what they have missed.
scheme: Two equal and opposite parallel forces form a couple — net force zero but net moment nonzero
The moment of a couple = one force × the perpendicular distance between the lines of action
A couple's turning effect is the same about any pivot — it cannot be cancelled by a pivot reaction
parts.answer: The forces do cancel as a resultant — but not as a turning effect. Equal, opposite and offset, they form a couple whose moment is F × (separation of the lines), and that twist acts about every point alike. A tap turns happily with zero net force: force balance and moment balance are separate accounts.

parts.move: solve simultaneous support reactions for a diver standing on a supported board
parts.prompt: A 3.0 m diving board of mass 30 kg is supported at one end by a pivot and 1.0 m along by a post. A 50 kg diver stands at the free end. Calculate the forces at the pivot and the post. (g = 9.81 m s⁻²)
scheme: Weights: board 294 N at 1.5 m; diver 490 N at 3.0 m
Moments about the pivot: R_post×1.0 = 294×1.5 + 490×3.0 = 441+1470 = 1911 N
Vertical balance: R_pivot = 294+490−1911 = −1127 N (pivot must hold the board down)
So post pushes up ~1.9 kN, pivot pulls down ~1.1 kN
parts.answer: Taking moments about the pivot: the post carries (294×1.5 + 490×3.0)/1.0 ≈ 1.91 kN upward. Vertical balance then makes the pivot force −1.13 kN — it pulls downward, which is why such boards are bolted down. The lever arms decide the split.

parts.move: transfer the base-of-support and moment-of-inertia intuition to balancing on a beam
parts.prompt: A gymnast on a beam carries a long pole and waves her arms when wobbling. Explain, in terms of the tipping condition and response time, how each trick helps.
scheme: Tipping requires the weight line to cross the foot's edge
The pole shifts the combined COM and adds rotational inertia, slowing the tip
Arm motions shift the COM back inside the base by moving mass
Both buy time and distance for the corrective reaction
parts.answer: Toppling is a race between the weight line and the base edge. The pole lengthens the system's inertia so a lean evolves slowly — more seconds to react — and moving it shifts the combined centre of mass back over the beam. Waving her arms is the same trick with her own mass: relocate the centre of mass faster than the wobble grows.

parts.move: transfer centre-of-mass tipping reasoning to a wheelchair on a slope
parts.prompt: A wheelchair tips backward on a steep ramp more easily than on level ground. Explain using the position of the combined centre of mass relative to the wheels' contact points.
scheme: On a slope the vertical through the COM shifts toward the rear wheels
Tipping begins when that line reaches the rear wheel contact line
A steeper slope or higher COM moves it over sooner
Anti-tip bars and leaning forward extend the base toward the front
parts.answer: Tipping starts when the plumb line from the centre of mass reaches the rear wheels' ground contacts. Tilting the slope tips the whole geometry: the vertical now leans rearward across the wheelbase, and steep enough puts it past the pivot. Leaning forward or adding anti-tip castors simply drags the base back under the line.

parts.move: combine resolution with moment balance at the foot when driving from blocks
parts.prompt: A sprinter pushes the rear block with a 700 N force directed 55° above the horizontal. The line of action passes 0.20 m above the ankle joint. Calculate the torque about the ankle due to the horizontal component of the force, and state its effect.
scheme: Horizontal component: 700 cos55° = 402 N
The vertical component's line passes through the ankle: no moment from it about the ankle
Torque = F_h × 0.20 = 80 N m
Dorsiflexion torque — the ankle must resist a powerful backward roll
parts.answer: Resolving the drive: 402 N horizontal. About the ankle that thrust — acting 0.20 m above the joint — rolls a torque of 80 N m into dorsiflexion. The block force doesn't just push the runner forward; it tries to fold the ankle, and the lower-leg muscles are the braces.

parts.move: combine centre-of-mass trajectory with energy conservation to estimate a jump height
parts.prompt: A high jumper's centre of mass stands 1.00 m above the ground at take-off. Her approach is 8.0 m s⁻¹ at 35° above horizontal. Calculate the rise of her centre of mass after take-off and the peak height it reaches, then explain how a 2.0 m bar is still plausible. (g = 9.81 m s⁻²)
scheme: The arch lets the body pass above a COM that slips below the bar — the bar can be above the COM's peak
parts.answer: The vertical velocity 8.0sin35° = 4.6 m s⁻¹ buys a rise of v²/2g = 1.07 m, lifting the centre of mass to about 2.07 m. A 2.0 m bar is thus at the COM's own peak height — achievable because the arched body threads over the bar while the centre of mass passes beneath it: two synoptic ideas, energy and geometry, making a jump look impossible.
